catalog_quote: THE STRUCTURE OF THE WORD 2.1. The structure of the word is very similar in both languages under discussion. Since stress plays no part in the phonetic system, the division into words of a spoken context must be somewhat arbitrary. The Kattang and Thangatti word is usually at least dis-syllabic and words of many syllables are frequent. The majority of monosyllabic noun and verb stems have a long vowel, especially when ... the word is pronounced with stress (that is as an independent unit), but short (or occasionally lengthened for emphasis) when pronounced without stress or as a component element (that is in most cases as an ... [Holmer & Holmer 1969, preface note 9:] ... njirtin(j) 'carries, carried', of which the second syllable ... stress was stronger on the last syllable than in, for instance, garra 'rain' ... stress is definitely not phonemic in either Kattang or Thangatti.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Holmer claims stress has no role in the Kattang (and Thangatti) sound system — i.e. no phonemic or systematic word stress is described; he uses this to explain why word division in connected speech is arbitrary. No positional rule is given in the visible snippet. The claim is echoed in a 1969 Linguistics review ('stress plays no part in the phonetic system, which implies that Holmer..'). Enright 1900 (opened, held by the project) marks accented syllables word by word but states no rule; a tally of his marks shows first-syllable marking in the large majority (244/258 disyllables, 116/149 trisyllables) with a minority of second- and final-syllable marks (bun-yil'-la 'struck', Bar-ra-kun' 'boomerang', boo-larng').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any visible text. Enright 1900 p.104 notes that 'where there are two accented syllables in the same word, they are both marked' (e.g. Yal'-lo-wal'-la, Koop'-pal-ee'-a-ni).
new_statements.exceptions: Holmer & Holmer 1969 snippet mentions a word where 'stress was stronger on the last syllable than in, for instance, garra..' (context not visible).
new_statements.domain_note: Holmer's remark concerns connected speech ('a spoken context') and word division; it is a negative statement about the role of stress, not a placement rule. Enright's marks are on citation forms and short sentences in an 1900 amateur transcription. The modern authority, Lissarrague 2010, could not be opened and may give a positive rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Holmer 1966 describes 'Kattang' (= Gathang; his informants Eddie Lobban and Fred Bugg, Port Stephens / Worimi area); Enright 1900 describes the 'Kutthung' dialect of the southern shore of Port Stephens (Warrimay/Worimi proper). Lissarrague 2010 treats Gathang as one language with three dialects (Birrbay, Guringay, Warrimay). All fall under wori1245.
